Forced celibacy doesn’t abolish anyone’s sexuality. For most people it eventually sends it somewhere weird. Why wouldn’t it?

windows.text: Modern life barely has an intermediate stage between being interested in somebody and getting sexually entangled. One old example is bundling, a mostly extinct practice now especially associated with the Amish, even though it existed much more widely. Courting couples could spend the night together in bed, usually clothed, with the idea that they could talk and be close without having sex, which sounds a lot like the missing middle I’m talking about.

windows.text: Well, it didn’t exactly solve the problem. In late-eighteenth-century New England, where lots of couples bundled, 30–40 percent of brides were already pregnant on their wedding day, so it wasn’t a very reliable way to keep courtship nonsexual.

windows.label: Human
windows.text: I’m not trying to bring bundling back. I just think we need some stage that everybody recognizes, where two people can explore tenderness and attraction without immediately sliding toward sex, moving in together, and a life bond.
